what_its_for: Icatibant is used to treat sudden attacks of a condition called hereditary angioedema (HAE). HAE causes episodes of severe swelling in parts of your body such as your hands, feet, face, throat, stomach, or genitals. This medicine helps stop the swelling during an attack.
how_to_take: Icatibant is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the stomach area (abdomen). Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to give yourself this injection at home. Always inject into a skin fold on your belly, avoiding areas that are bruised, red, tender, or scarred. Use a new prefilled syringe for each dose and never reuse syringes or needles. Pinch the skin, insert the needle at a 45- to 90-degree angle, inject slowly, and then remove the needle. Press gently on the injection site with a cotton ball but do not rub.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 30 mg (one prefilled syringe) injected under the skin as soon as you notice an HAE attack starting. If your symptoms do not improve after 6 hours, you may give a second 30 mg dose. If symptoms still continue, a third dose may be given 6 hours after the second dose. Do not take more than 3 doses (90 mg total) in any 24-hour period. Only use this medicine when you are having an attack, not every day.
missed_dose: Icatibant is not taken on a regular daily schedule — it is only used when you are having an HAE attack. There is no missed dose concern in the traditional sense. If you feel an attack coming on, use your dose as soon as possible. Always carry your medication with you so it is available when you need it.
storage: Store icatibant at room temperature between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in the original packaging to protect it from light. Do not use it if the solution looks cloudy, discolored, or contains particles. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Check the expiration date before each use and properly dispose of any expired or used syringes in a sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are taking ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril, enalapril, or ramipril) for blood pressure or heart conditions, because icatibant may make those medicines less effective. Avoid injecting into skin that is irritated, bruised, or infected. Do not share your syringes or medication with anyone else.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency medical help right away if: your swelling is in your throat or airway and you are having trouble breathing or swallowing (this is a life-threatening emergency); your symptoms do not improve or get worse after using the full three doses within 24 hours; you have serious injection site reactions such as severe pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site; you feel dizzy, faint, or have a rapid heartbeat; or you experience any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Most people start to feel relief within 2 hours after the injection. Swelling usually begins to go down within a few hours. The full effect may take several hours. If you do not notice any improvement within 6 hours of your first dose, give a second dose as directed.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Use with caution. Your doctor will monitor you carefully as there is limited data in older patients. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Use only if clearly needed and your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk. Breastfeeding: It is not known if icatibant passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children and teenagers (under 18): Safety and effectiveness in patients younger than 18 years of age have not been established. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustment is currently recommended, but always inform your doctor of any kidney or liver conditions you have.
